text: Sri Prakasa (3 August 1890 – 23 June 1971) was an Indian politician, freedom-fighter, and administrator. He was born in Varanasi on 3 August 1890 to Bhagwan Das and received his early education at Central Hindu Boys' School (C.H.B.S.) Varanasi, graduating from Cambridge. He participated in the Indian independence movement and was arrested during the Quit India Movement, serving in jail from 1942 to 1944. After independence, he served as an administrator and cabinet minister. In August 1947, he was appointed India's first High Commissioner to Pakistan, a position he held until 1949. During this period, Pakistan faced communal riots, and Sri Prakasa managed the influx of refugees into India and the granting of Indian citizenship to migrants, while also representing India's diplomatic interests during Pakistan's invasion of Kashmir. He served as Governor of Assam from 16 February 1949 to 27 May 1949, during which time serious disturbances occurred in the eastern parts of the province inhabited by the Mizo Hill tribes. To address the unrest, he promised sufficient autonomy, leading to the establishment of a Lushai Hills Advisory Council, and during his tenure, secured the accession of Manipur. In 1952, he was elected to the Lok Sabha from Prayagraj but was soon appointed Governor of Madras, serving from 1952 to 1956. While in this role, he made a controversial decision to invite C. Rajagopalachari to form a Congress government despite the party lacking a majority and Rajagopalachari not being an elected member of the assembly; Rajagopalachari requested Prakasa to nominate him to the assembly, bypassing the standard election process. Rajagopalachari resigned after two years due to strong opposition within the party. P.C. Alexander, a former governor of Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra, criticized the actions of both the governor and the chief minister as a serious breach of democratic principles. Sri Prakasa later served as Governor of Bombay. He died in 1971 at the age of 80.
